title: Tyler’s water
lead: Tyler owns its water and sewer system (Tyler Water Utilities, a city department), paid for by water and sewer bills. Rural Smith County is served largely by water supply corporations — nonprofits owned by their members.

facts.v: Lake Tyler and Lake Tyler East feed the Golden Road plant; Lake Palestine feeds the Lake Palestine plant.
The City of Tyler (Texas public water system 2120004).
An estimated 2,084,630,147 gallons in 2025 — over 2 billion gallons — per the water-loss audit Tyler filed with the Texas Water Development Board.

Under a 2017 federal consent decree after years of sewer overflows: a $563,000 penalty, and fixes EPA estimated could cost more than $65 million. Overflows are down from about 15 to 6.9 per 100 miles of pipe (50 in 2025); the goal is under 5.

facts.v: Of about 40,000 service lines, 142 are lead (0.37%) and 3,843 are galvanized steel needing replacement (9.91%). The city plans to finish replacements by 2037.

facts.v: For 2026–27 the base water rate stays at $3.75 per 1,000 gallons for the first 25,000 gallons; the budget cash-funds $13.6 million of water and wastewater projects.
Jackson Water Supply Corporation, for example, is member-owned and board-managed, serving the Chapel Hill and Arp area since 1967 from five deep Carrizo-Wilcox wells.

quality.lead: Tyler’s 2025 report lists no violation notices.

rows.value: 0 ppb at the 90th percentile (highest single test 6.55)
rows.note: No homes over the action level.

quality.violation: Total organic carbon removal met every requirement in 2025.
quality.inspection: Sewer plants: a June 2024 storm knocked out power at the Westside plant and 3,953,070 gallons of sewage reached Black Fork Creek. Separately, the state fined the Southside plant $23,250 for ammonia and solids over its limits (Dec 2023–Apr 2024) during a $16 million upgrade; most was offset by an environmental project and $4,650 was paid.
quality.note: The city’s report doesn’t include PFAS (“forever chemical”) results (Docket #8).

fits.name: Find the water we’re losing
fits.why: Over 2 billion gallons were lost in 2025 — water already pumped and treated. What share of production that is, and what it costs, isn’t stated in the report (Docket #9). Leak-finding meters are the proven first step.

fits.name: Finish the sewer fixes, then keep them fixed
fits.why: The overflow rate has dropped by more than half since 2017; the consent decree’s goal is under 5 per 100 miles. Backup power at plants is the lesson of the 2024 spill.

fits.name: Replace the 3,985 lead and galvanized lines
fits.why: Federal lead-pipe money flows through the state revolving fund — the sooner it’s used, the sooner the 2037 target moves up.

fits.name: Protect the lakes
fits.why: All of Tyler’s treated water starts in three lakes; keeping their watersheds healthy is the cheapest treatment there is.

question: Who pays for the sewer fixes, and how much have they cost so far against EPA’s $65 million estimate? The records we have don’t total it yet (Docket #10).
